words.definition: formal approval or praise
words.nuance: Formal; often from an authority or the public.
examples: The proposal won the approbation of the review board.
She worked hard, but never for the sake of approbation.

words.definition: to give official permission or approval for; also, to impose a penalty on
words.nuance: A contronym: it can mean both to approve and to punish. Context decides.
examples: The committee refused to sanction the use of public funds for the project.
The league may sanction the team for breaking its spending rules.

words.definition: a speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly
words.nuance: More elevated than 'tribute'; unlike a eulogy, its subject needn't have died.
examples: The retiring dean received a lavish encomium from her colleagues.
His review reads less like criticism than an encomium to the director.

words.definition: a public speech or text in praise of someone or something
words.nuance: Often implies elaborate or excessive praise.
examples: The biography is less a history than a panegyric to its subject.
At the banquet, the senator delivered a long panegyric on the city's founders.

words.definition: to scold or criticize someone angrily
words.nuance: Angry and prolonged; often in front of others.
examples: The coach would berate players for every missed tackle.
Don't berate yourself over one bad exam.

words.definition: to express sharp disapproval of someone because of their behavior
words.nuance: Also a noun: 'a sharp rebuke.'
examples: The judge chose to rebuke the lawyer in open court.
Her quiet rebuke silenced the room.

words.definition: to publicly denounce as wrong or harmful
words.nuance: Public, often on moral grounds; the target is usually a practice, not a person.
examples: Environmental groups decry the use of single-use plastics.
Many critics decry the decline of public libraries.

words.definition: to speak or write about someone in an abusively disparaging way
words.nuance: Stronger than criticize: it aims to make someone look like a villain.
examples: The tabloids continued to vilify the witness for months.
It is easier to vilify immigrants than to fix the economy.

words.definition: to speak about someone in a spitefully critical way
words.nuance: As an adjective it means evil or harmful ('a malign influence').
examples: Critics continue to malign the policy without reading it.
It is unfair to malign a whole profession for one scandal.

words.definition: to attack or ridicule publicly
words.nuance: From the wooden frame in which offenders were exposed to public scorn.
examples: Columnists continued to pillory the minister for his remarks.
Satirists love to pillory the powerful.

words.definition: making a show of being morally superior to others
words.nuance: Implies hypocrisy or smugness, not real virtue.
examples: Nobody enjoyed his sanctimonious lectures about saving money.
The editorial struck readers as sanctimonious rather than persuasive.

words.definition: unable to be appeased or pacified; relentless
words.nuance: Often of enemies, anger, or opposition.
examples: The senator was an implacable foe of the new tax.
Her implacable anger outlasted every apology.

words.definition: abrupt or offhand in speech or manner
words.nuance: Short to the point of rudeness; about manner more than word count.
examples: The clerk's brusque manner discouraged further questions.
He gave a brusque nod and walked away.

words.definition: modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence
words.nuance: Unlike reticent (choosing not to speak), diffident is about low confidence.
examples: The diffident student rarely raised her hand, though she knew the answers.
He was diffident about sharing his poems.

words.definition: high-sounding but with little meaning; inflated
words.nuance: Describes language or speakers, not loudness.
examples: The candidate's bombastic speeches promised everything and explained nothing.
Strip away the bombastic language and the plan is quite modest.

words.definition: pompous or extravagant in language, style, or manner
words.nuance: Meant to impress; the grand words exceed the content.
examples: The grandiloquent opening of the report hid a simple message.
His grandiloquent toasts amused some guests and bored others.

words.definition: tediously pompous or bombastic in style; also, swollen
words.nuance: In writing, heavy and overblown; literally, swollen with fluid.
examples: Even experts struggled through the turgid prose of the manual.
The river ran turgid after a week of rain.

words.definition: enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining
words.nuance: From the Stoic philosophers; endurance rather than mere calm.
examples: She bore the bad news with stoic calm.
The stoic farmer said little about the failed harvest.

words.definition: mental calmness and evenness of temper, especially in difficulty
examples: She accepted the verdict with equanimity.
Meditation helped him keep his equanimity during the crisis.

words.definition: self-confidence or assurance, especially in a demanding situation
words.nuance: Usually 'with aplomb': handling something difficult smoothly.
examples: The young pianist performed the difficult piece with aplomb.
She handled the hostile questions with aplomb.

words.definition: sparing or economical with money or food
words.nuance: Positive or neutral, unlike stingy or parsimonious.
examples: Years of frugal living let them buy the house outright.
Dinner was a frugal meal of bread and soup.

words.definition: to declare someone free from guilt, obligation, or punishment
words.nuance: Also used for religious forgiveness and for releasing someone from a duty.
examples: The inquiry did not absolve the company of responsibility.
No apology can absolve him of what he did.

words.definition: cheerful and full of energy
words.nuance: Literally 'boiling over': bubbling enthusiasm.
examples: The ebullient host greeted every guest by name.
Investors were ebullient after the strong earnings report.

words.definition: filled with lively energy and excitement; also, growing profusely
examples: The exuberant crowd poured onto the field after the win.
Her exuberant paintings burst with color.

words.definition: lacking inspiration or excitement; dull
words.nuance: GRE trap: in this sense it has nothing to do with walking.
examples: The film's pedestrian script wasted a talented cast.
After a brilliant first chapter, the novel turns pedestrian.

words.definition: tending to obstruct or harm; unfriendly or hostile
words.nuance: Usually 'inimical to': harmful to.
examples: Constant surveillance is inimical to creative work.
The climate there is inimical to most crops.

words.definition: producing good effects; beneficial, often through an unpleasant experience
words.nuance: A 'salutary lesson' is a painful but useful one.
examples: The failed launch was a salutary lesson in testing.
A short walk had a salutary effect on her mood.

words.definition: health-giving; also, pleasant and respectable
words.nuance: Of climates, air, or neighborhoods.
examples: Patients were sent to the coast for its salubrious climate.
The office moved to a more salubrious part of town.

words.definition: to stir up or instigate trouble or rebellion
words.nuance: Almost always negative: unrest, dissent, revolution.
examples: Agents were accused of trying to foment unrest in the region.
Rumors on social media helped foment the riot.

words.definition: hesitating or doubting; also, not to be relied on
words.nuance: Can describe a person (doubtful) or a thing (suspect): 'a dubious claim.'
examples: She was dubious about the offer's promised returns.
The study relied on data of dubious quality.

words.definition: of something undesirable, widespread; also, full of
words.nuance: Usually about something bad: 'rife with corruption.'
examples: The old regime was rife with corruption.
Rumors were rife that the company would be sold.

words.definition: friendly and cheerful
examples: Our genial host made everyone feel at home.
Despite his fame, he remained genial and approachable.

words.definition: done with or employing great care and thoroughness
examples: The restoration took years of painstaking work.
Her painstaking research uncovered the original letters.

words.definition: very careful and thorough; also, careful to do what is morally right
words.nuance: Two senses: precise attention, and strict honesty.
examples: The auditors kept scrupulous records of every payment.
A scrupulous lawyer would never hide that evidence.

words.definition: to hinder or impede the movement or progress of
examples: Heavy snow continued to hamper rescue efforts.
A lack of funding will hamper the research.

words.definition: to burden or restrict; to impede
words.nuance: Also of debts: 'a property encumbered by loans.'
examples: Strict rules encumber small businesses with paperwork.
The new owners did not want to encumber the company with more debt.

words.definition: to remove a need or difficulty; to prevent by anticipating
words.nuance: Not 'make obvious': to obviate the need for X is to make X unnecessary.
examples: A simple checklist can obviate the need for costly repairs.
Planning ahead will obviate most of these delays.

words.definition: to make a problem or difficulty worse
words.nuance: GRE trap: in this sense it means 'worsen,' not 'combine.'
examples: Lying about the mistake will only compound the problem.
Bad weather served to compound the delays.

words.definition: to win or regain the favor of someone by doing something that pleases them
words.nuance: Often of gods or powerful figures.
examples: Ancient farmers offered sacrifices to propitiate the gods.
The CEO tried to propitiate angry shareholders with a dividend.

words.definition: to diminish or put at rest a fear, suspicion, or worry
words.nuance: Usually of fears, concerns, or suspicions.
examples: The mayor tried to allay fears about the water supply.
Nothing she said could allay his suspicion.

words.definition: to use ambiguous language to conceal the truth or avoid committing oneself
examples: When asked directly, the spokesperson continued to equivocate.
Don't equivocate: tell us whether you support the plan.

words.definition: the use of trickery to achieve a political, financial, or legal purpose
examples: The election was marred by chicanery at several polling stations.
Investigators uncovered years of accounting chicanery.

words.definition: deceit used to achieve one's goal
examples: The spy obtained the documents by subterfuge.
Rather than resort to subterfuge, she asked for the data openly.

words.definition: sly or cunning intelligence
words.nuance: Guileless means innocent and trusting.
examples: In the fable, the fox wins by guile rather than strength.
She negotiated with charm and guile.

words.definition: clever or cunning devices used to trick or deceive; also, skill
examples: Her performance was moving precisely because it lacked artifice.
The ad relied on artifice rather than evidence.

words.definition: the use of clever but false arguments to deceive
words.nuance: From the Sophists, teachers accused of winning arguments rather than finding truth.
examples: His defense of the policy was clever sophistry, not evidence.
Students learned to spot sophistry in political speeches.

words.definition: having or showing no moral principles; not honest or fair
examples: Unscrupulous landlords raised rents on struggling tenants.
The scheme was designed by an unscrupulous broker.

words.definition: lacking energy or enthusiasm
examples: The heat left everyone listless by noon.
After a listless first half, the team rallied.

words.definition: showing a casual lack of concern
words.nuance: Carefree and often charming, where apathetic is dull.
examples: He gave an insouciant shrug when told he was late.
Her insouciant attitude toward deadlines worried her editor.

words.definition: causing or likely to cause an argument; also, given to arguing
words.nuance: Usually of issues: 'a contentious topic.'
examples: Immigration remains a contentious issue.
The contentious meeting ran past midnight.

words.definition: sharp and forthright, especially in criticism; also, sour
words.nuance: Often of wit or remarks.
examples: The critic was famous for her acerbic wit.
His acerbic emails made him few friends.

words.definition: sarcastic in a scathing and bitter way; also, able to burn by chemical action
examples: She ignored his caustic remarks about her cooking.
Wear gloves when handling caustic chemicals.

words.definition: having or showing a sharp or critical quality; biting
words.nuance: Usually of humor: dark and cutting.
examples: The play is full of mordant humor about office life.
His mordant commentary spared no one.

words.definition: having or showing an excessive willingness to serve or please others
examples: The servile courtiers agreed with every word the king said.
She refused to adopt a servile tone with clients.

words.definition: excessively flattering or ingratiating; oily
words.nuance: Suggests insincere, slippery charm.
examples: The unctuous salesman complimented everything we touched.
His unctuous praise made the guests uncomfortable.

words.definition: to accept something reluctantly but without protest
words.nuance: Usually 'acquiesce in' or 'acquiesce to.'
examples: The board finally chose to acquiesce to the union's demands.
She did not agree, but she would acquiesce rather than fight.

words.definition: to cease to resist an opponent or demand; to surrender
words.nuance: Implies giving in after resistance.
examples: After weeks of protests, the government chose to capitulate.
The garrison refused to capitulate despite the siege.

words.definition: without a clearly defined shape or form
examples: The plan remained an amorphous set of goals.
An amorphous blob of clay sat on the wheel.

words.definition: hard or impossible to understand; also, not transparent
examples: The contract was written in opaque legal language.
Critics say the selection process is opaque.

words.definition: to make something greater by adding to it; to increase
examples: She tutors on weekends to augment her income.
The team plans to augment its staff before launch.

words.definition: to begin to grow or increase rapidly; to flourish
words.nuance: Commonly as 'burgeoning': a burgeoning industry.
examples: Small businesses began to burgeon after the new bridge opened.
Interest in electric cars continues to burgeon.

words.definition: to increase rapidly in number; to multiply
examples: Food trucks began to proliferate downtown.
Misinformation tends to proliferate during a crisis.

words.definition: excessively concerned with minor details or rules; showing off learning
examples: He was pedantic about the difference between 'less' and 'fewer.'
The lecture was accurate but painfully pedantic.

words.definition: intended to teach, often with a moral lesson; sometimes preachy
words.nuance: Neutral (educational) or negative (lecturing).
examples: The novel's didactic tone put off many readers.
Fables have a didactic purpose: each ends with a moral.

words.definition: having, showing, or done with good judgment
words.nuance: Often of decisions or use: 'judicious use of resources.'
examples: With judicious use of the budget, the school bought new laptops.
A judicious editor cut the weakest chapters.

words.definition: having knowledge of events before they happen; farsighted
examples: Her prescient warning about the housing market went unheeded.
In hindsight, the essay seems remarkably prescient.

words.definition: filled or well supplied with something
words.nuance: Usually 'replete with.'
examples: The report is replete with useful charts.
Her memoir is replete with funny stories.

words.definition: unnecessary, especially through being more than enough
examples: The editor cut every superfluous word.
With the new software, the extra step became superfluous.

words.definition: irrelevant or unrelated to the subject; coming from outside
examples: Remove extraneous information before submitting the report.
The microphone picked up extraneous noise from the street.

words.definition: uncalled for; lacking good reason; also, free of charge
words.nuance: Mostly negative: 'gratuitous violence.'
examples: Critics objected to the film's gratuitous violence.
The final remark was a gratuitous insult.

words.definition: bold and without shame
words.nuance: Bold in a bad way; compare audacious, which can be admiring.
examples: It was a brazen attempt to rewrite history.
The thieves were brazen enough to return the next day.

words.definition: excessive confidence or boldness; audacity
words.nuance: Usually 'had the temerity to.'
examples: He had the temerity to criticize the host's cooking at dinner.
She admired the temerity of the young lawyer.

words.definition: done, made, or acting suddenly or without careful thought
words.nuance: As a verb it means to cause something to happen suddenly ('precipitate a crisis').
examples: The board warned against a precipitate decision.
Their precipitate retreat left the supplies behind.

words.definition: inexperienced and immature (of a young person)
examples: As a callow youth, he thought he knew everything.
The callow recruits were nervous on their first patrol.

words.definition: childishly silly and trivial
examples: The comedy relied on puerile jokes.
Their puerile insults embarrassed everyone in the room.

words.definition: the highest point in the development of something; climax
words.nuance: Literally the point in an orbit farthest from Earth.
examples: The empire reached its apogee under its third ruler.
Many consider the album the apogee of her career.

words.definition: to become less intense or widespread
examples: We waited for the storm to abate.
The protests showed no sign they would abate.

words.definition: expressed clearly; easy to understand; also, thinking clearly
examples: The textbook offers a lucid explanation of the theory.
In a lucid moment, the patient recognized his daughter.

words.definition: clear, logical, and convincing
words.nuance: About arguments: persuasive because well reasoned.
examples: She made a cogent argument for delaying the vote.
The report offers no cogent reasons for the change.

words.definition: feeling or expressing remorse for having done wrong
examples: The contrite student apologized to the whole class.
He did not seem contrite about the damage he caused.

words.definition: feeling sorrow and regret for having done wrong
words.nuance: Also a noun: a person who repents.
examples: The penitent driver visited the family he had injured.
His letter struck a penitent tone.

words.definition: resolutely or dutifully firm and unwavering
examples: She thanked her family for their steadfast support.
He was steadfast in his refusal to sign.

words.definition: loyal, reliable, and hardworking; also, strongly built
words.nuance: Also a noun: 'a party stalwart.'
examples: She was a stalwart supporter of the library for forty years.
Even stalwart fans began to lose patience.

words.definition: treating all rivals or sides equally; fair and unbiased
examples: The dispute needs an impartial judge.
Reporters are expected to stay impartial.

words.definition: not influenced by personal advantage; impartial
words.nuance: GRE trap: not the same as 'uninterested' (bored).
examples: A disinterested party should review the contract.
She offered disinterested advice, since she stood to gain nothing.

words.definition: relevant to a subject under consideration
words.nuance: Usually 'germane to.'
examples: Her comment was not germane to the discussion.
The judge ruled the evidence germane to the case.

words.definition: relevant or applicable to a particular matter
examples: She asked a pertinent question about the budget.
Please include all pertinent information in the form.

words.definition: designed to impress or attract notice; showy
examples: The mansion was an ostentatious display of new money.
They lived modestly, avoiding anything ostentatious.

words.definition: tending to attract attention through exuberance, confidence, and style
words.nuance: Less critical than ostentatious; can be admiring.
examples: The singer was known for her flamboyant costumes.
His flamboyant style made the lecture memorable.

words.definition: obtrusively bright and showy; lurid
words.nuance: Usually of colors or decoration.
examples: The room was painted in garish colors.
Garish neon signs lined the strip.

words.definition: severe or strict in manner; also, plain and without decoration
words.nuance: In economics, 'austerity' means deep spending cuts.
examples: The monks lived an austere life of work and prayer.
The museum's austere design keeps attention on the art.

words.definition: characterized by severe self-discipline and avoidance of indulgence
words.nuance: Also a noun: a person who lives this way.
examples: He followed an ascetic diet of rice and water.
The ascetic monks owned nothing but their robes.

words.definition: very old or old-fashioned; no longer in everyday use
examples: Some archaic laws were never removed from the books.
The poem's archaic language puzzled students.

words.definition: old-fashioned or outdated
words.nuance: Usually critical: too old to be useful.
examples: The hospital still relies on antiquated equipment.
His antiquated views on women surprised the panel.

words.definition: just coming into existence and beginning to show promise
examples: The country's nascent tech industry needs investment.
The movement was still nascent when it lost its leader.

words.definition: in an initial stage; beginning to happen or develop
words.nuance: Often of problems: 'incipient decay.'
examples: Doctors caught the disease at an incipient stage.
Economists noticed incipient signs of a recession.

words.definition: inborn; natural
examples: She has an innate ability to put people at ease.
Some argue that the capacity for language is innate.

words.definition: existing as a permanent, essential, or characteristic attribute
examples: Every investment carries some inherent risk.
The problem is inherent in the design.

words.definition: belonging naturally; essential
words.nuance: Often contrasted with extrinsic: intrinsic motivation, intrinsic value.
examples: The painting has little intrinsic value but great sentimental value.
Curiosity is an intrinsic part of learning.

words.definition: understood or implied without being stated
examples: Her silence was taken as tacit approval.
There was a tacit understanding that no one would mention the merger.

words.definition: implied though not plainly expressed; also, absolute
words.nuance: 'Implicit trust' means complete trust.
examples: The criticism was implicit in her question.
Studies of implicit bias examine unconscious attitudes.

words.definition: diverse in character or content
words.nuance: Opposite: homogeneous (all of one kind).
examples: The class was a heterogeneous group of ages and backgrounds.
Granite is a heterogeneous mixture of minerals.

words.definition: essentially different in kind; not able to be compared
words.nuance: Not to be confused with 'desperate.'
examples: The project brought together disparate groups of researchers.
She wove disparate elements into a single story.
